one_liner: General-purpose lossless compressor beating zlib/deflate on speed and ratio, with tunable levels and negative fast modes.
what_it_does: Zstandard is an in-memory lossless data compressor for files, streams, and network payloads, aimed at replacing zlib/deflate at similar or better ratio with much higher throughput. It exposes a C API with a simple one-shot form (ZSTD_compress/ZSTD_decompress), an explicit-context form for reuse, and a streaming API, plus a CLI that reads/writes its own .zst container (RFC 8878) as well as .gz/.xz/.lz4. It is not wire-compatible with zlib; adopting it means changing the compressed format, not just relinking.
how_it_is_fast: Compression uses selectable match-finder strategies per level, from cheap hash-chain/greedy search at low levels up to binary-tree/optimal parsing at high levels, so speed vs ratio is a single tunable knob (including negative --fast=# levels that skip expensive search entirely). The entropy stage uses FSE (tANS) and Huff0, which decode faster than classic Huffman/zlib entropy coding. On x86-64 the library auto-dispatches to BMI2 instructions at runtime when available, mainly speeding up the decoder; optional dictionary training (ZDICT) amortizes the cost of small, similarly-shaped inputs.
when_to_use: General file/stream compression where you want a better ratio than zlib at several times the throughput
Workloads needing a single tunable speed/ratio knob, from --fast=# (skip ratio for max speed) up to level 22 (max ratio)
Many small, structurally similar records (e.g. JSON/API payloads) via a trained dictionary, where per-item ratio would otherwise be poor
Large-payload compression that can use multiple threads (built with ZSTD_MULTITHREAD + pthread)
Codebases needing a permissive-or-copyleft license choice (dual BSD-3-Clause / GPLv2)
when_not_to_use: You need byte-compatible zlib/deflate/gzip output for an existing wire protocol or file format — zstd's container is a different, RFC 8878 format
You need the best possible ratio regardless of CPU cost — the README's own table doesn't include xz, a stronger-ratio baseline it lists as uncompared here
You're decompressing untrusted archives via the CLI's recursive mode: a crafted circular symlink can hang `zstd -d -r -f` (open issue #4081)
You need the experimental/advanced API surface (behind ZSTD_STATIC_LINKING_ONLY) in a dynamically-linked build — it's explicitly static-link-only and unstable across versions
You're on a toolchain where strict C90 portability doesn't matter and you'd rather have a simpler, smaller single-strategy codec

integration.form: static lib | shared lib | source-drop (Makefile is the reference build; CMake, Meson, Buck, Bazel, and VS project files are also maintained)
integration.dependencies: none for core library; POSIX pthread required only if built with ZSTD_MULTITHREAD for multithreaded compression
integration.min_toolchain: strict C90 C (per CONTRIBUTING.md); no C99/C++ requirement for the library itself
integration.platforms: portable C90 baseline runs anywhere; x86-64 gets optional runtime BMI2 dispatch (auto-detected, not required); aarch64 supported; Windows via VS2008+/CMake; macOS Universal2 (x86_64/arm64) build documented
integration.thread_safety: CCtx/DCtx are not thread-safe — use one context per thread for parallel calls. A created ZSTD_CDict is read-only and safe to share across threads concurrently. Default `make lib` builds a multithreaded dynamic library but a single-threaded static library; `lib-mt`/`lib-nomt` targets force one or the other.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — same in-memory/streaming compression API shape as zlib (one-shot and streaming calls) but a different, non-interoperable wire format, so callers must change format, not just swap the library

gotchas: Static and dynamic library builds default to different threading modes (single- vs multi-threaded); mismatched expectations here are a common build-config surprise
Advanced/experimental API (unlocked via ZSTD_STATIC_LINKING_ONLY) is explicitly forbidden with dynamic linking because its ABI is unstable
CLI recursive decompress can hang on a crafted circular symlink (open issue #4081) — a library-embedding concern only if you shell out to the CLI
Open performance-regression report (#4587) for level 18 after an internal API v2 change, unresolved as of this session
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick zstd over LZ4 when ratio matters more than raw peak speed: zstd -1 gets 2.896 ratio at 510/1550 MB/s vs LZ4's 2.101 ratio at 780/4970 MB/s in the same README table. Pick LZ4 instead when you need decompression well above 2 GB/s or compression above ~700 MB/s and can accept a much lower ratio.
verified_claims_summary: zstd 1.5.7 -1 measured 510 MB/s compression and 1550 MB/s decompression at ratio 2.896, vs zlib 1.3.1 -1 at 105 MB/s / 390 MB/s and ratio 2.743, in the project's own README Benchmarks table (lzbench, gcc 14.2.0, Silesia corpus, single-threaded, Core i7-9700K @ 4.9GHz, Ubuntu 24.04). The lzbench project's own README independently corroborates a similar zstd-vs-zlib gap on different hardware (AMD EPYC 9554, zstd 1.5.6 -1 at 422/1347 MB/s vs zlib 1.3.1 -1 at 93.0/323 MB/s).
status_note: Actively maintained (last commit 2026-09-18 on branch 'dev'), reference implementation of RFC 8878 used in the Linux kernel, Chromium, FreeBSD, and PostgreSQL; usability is 'copyable' and it is dual-licensed BSD-3-Clause OR GPLv2.
